title: How do you structure a case where the client needs to cut costs?
description: "How can the client cut costs?" The client needs to cut costs, often by a target percentage. The structure, the first question to ask, and practice prompts wi
hook: Cost cases can feel endless, because every business has hundreds of costs. The trick is to sort them into a few groups, find the biggest ones, and look there first. Here is a clean way to structure it.
body:
When you will use it

The client needs to cut costs, often by a target percentage.

This is a diagnose question: "Why is this happening, and how do we fix it?" Break the problem into parts that add up, find which part moved, then fix that part. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Which costs are in scope, and what must not suffer (quality, safety, service)?

One good question at the start can halve the work. It tells you where to look, and it shows the interviewer you are thinking about the client, not reciting a list.

The structure

  • Need less
    • Stop the activity (close a branch · move to self-service)
    • Do less of it (lower a service level, like free delivery)
  • Use less per unit
    • Cut waste and rework
    • Get more output per person or machine
  • Pay less per unit
    • Switch to cheaper inputs or outsource (rail instead of air freight)
    • Negotiate better prices

Say it out loud as a short sentence per branch, then say which branch you would look at first and why. That last part, your hypothesis, is what most candidates forget.

Make it your own

Cost = how much we do × resources per unit × price per resource. Each branch cuts one factor. Start with the biggest cost lines, and protect the costs that bring in revenue.

Interviewers can tell when a structure has been memorised. Swap the general words for words about this client: not "costs", but "fuel and crew costs" for an airline.

Practise with real prompts

Read each prompt, take two minutes to sketch your own structure, then compare.

1. A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show a model structure
  • Number of returns: Online orders: did sales grow?; Return rate by category, size, brand; serial returners
  • Cost per return: Shipping, handling, refurbishing; Items that can no longer be sold
  • Why customers return: Fit and sizing, photos and descriptions; Ordering several sizes on purpose
  • Policy: Free returns, return window; Charging, store returns, exchanges first

Where to start: Orders × return rate × cost per return: find which grew, then the categories driving it.

The trap: Listing policies to change without first splitting the number of returns from cost per return.

2. A retail bank wants to cut operating costs by 15% in two years.

Show a model structure
  • Branches: Number, size and use of branches; Staffing vs footfall
  • Operations: Back office: payments, lending, account opening; Automation and outsourcing
  • Technology: Old systems, licences, data centres; Duplicate apps and vendors
  • Support functions: HR, finance, procurement; Spans of control and layers

Where to start: The biggest cost pool first: usually staff in branches and operations.

The trap: Listing cost ideas without sizing the cost base, so you can't say which matters.

3. A food-delivery start-up is burning $5M a month. Where would you cut?

Show a model structure
  • Unit economics per order: Commission, delivery fee, courier cost; Discounts and refunds
  • Marketing: Cost to acquire a customer vs their value; Promotions with no repeat
  • Cities: Profit by city; Exit or pause the weakest
  • Fixed costs: Head office, tech, offices; Hiring plans

Where to start: Profit per order by city: losing money on every order can't be fixed with volume.

The trap: Cutting head office first when the loss is in every order.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. You can see this tree drawn step by step, and every other core framework, on the free frameworks page.
